info.bio:
The Streets es el projecto de Mike Skinner nacido en Birmingham, Reino Unido el 27 de noviembre de 1978, y afincado en el Norte de Londres.

Original Pirate Material(02), clásico absoluto, destapó a Mike Skinner como un enorme productor. Con aquel referencial debut, se nos presentaba un fresquísimo cronista social que definía sin artificios un concepto tan complejo como es “vivir en Inglaterra”. Bajo el alias The Streets, influenciado desde su infancia por De La Soul y Beastie Boys

podcast.title: Mike Skinner's Lyrical Style
podcast.body: Mike Skinner, the leader of The Streets, is highly regarded for his observational, conversational, and colloquial lyrical style. His work, particularly on the album "A Grand Don't Come for Free," was a significant influence on Alex Turner's songwriting.

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Pure and Good Rap Outside Traditional Hip Hop
podcast.body: The Streets are acknowledged for producing "very pure and good" rap, even while being considered outside the traditional hip hop cultural framework by some critics. This view recognizes rap's evolution beyond its original cultural context, allowing for diverse stylistic and thematic interpretations. "mucho rap pero es blanco es como de streets o el p hacen rap si hacen un rap muy puro además y muy bueno están englobadas una entrada cultura hip hop personalmente creo que no ni en estilo ni en tipo de rítmase ni en estructuras ni temáticas ni en comportamiento ni en nada"

podcast.title: Rap Disconnected from Hip Hop Culture
podcast.body: The Streets are presented as an example of "white rap" that, despite its quality, some critics argue has little to do with the classical hip hop cultural movement. This perspective suggests that rap, as a singing method, can exist and thrive independently of the broader cultural tenets of hip hop. "poco tienen que ver con la cultura clásica del hip hop como puede ser el p o como puede ser de streets lo consideran de mis esticiones del hip hop pero dentro del hip hop"

xref.title: Montreal Arrival and Death Threats (1964)
xref.body: The Beatles' arrival at Dorval Airport for their only visit to La Belle province mirrored the scenes at other tour stops, with hordes of screaming fans. However, their time in Quebec was significantly marred by death threats from French Canadian separatists, specifically the FLQ, leading to the presence of police sharpshooters at the Montreal Forum on St. Catherine Street for their two concerts. "Their arrival at the Dorval Airport mirrored what happened at every stop on their tour. Hordes of screaming fans at the airport throngs of fans lying the streets, clutching magazines and singing their favorite Beatles songs."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: "Sabotage" Music Video (1994) – 70s Crime Show Parody
xref.body: The music video for "Sabotage" was directed by Spike Jonze, who had previously photographed skateboarders, and featured a concept devised by the Beastie Boys themselves. It parodied 1970s crime shows, complete with all the clichés and "bad moustaches." The video was shot with a skeleton crew, fitting everyone into one van, and without permits, allowing for quick filming on the streets of Los Angeles with a relatively tiny budget compared to other videos of the era. "The Beastie Boys came up with the concept that parodied 70's crime shows, complete with all the clichés and bad moustaches."

xref.title: "Science Teacher" Role for "Where the Streets Have No Name"
xref.body: During the recording of U2's "Where the Streets Have No Name," he used a large blackboard and a pointer, acting as a "science teacher," to visually guide the band members, particularly the rhythm section, through the complex time signature changes (from 6/8 to 4/4) in the song's intro. "I was in, I was the science teacher so I had the pointer and I pointed at the chord changes as they came around."

xref.title: Collapse Backstage at "Lazarus" Musical
xref.body: In early December 2015, after attending a performance of his musical "Lazarus" and meeting with the director, Bowie collapsed backstage. He subsequently regained some strength and was seen on the streets of New York as late as his 69th birthday, January 8th, 2016. "In early December 2015, Bowie attended a performance of his musical Lazarus. After meeting with the director, he collapsed backstage."

xref.title: Early Life and Tough Demeanor
xref.body: Born Lizzie Douglas in Louisiana in 1897, Memphis Mini ran away from home at the age of 13 to play guitar on the street corners of Memphis. When busking didn't provide enough income, she reportedly worked as a prostitute, and she was known for her toughness, unafraid to fight and capable of using a knife or pistol if necessary. "She was tough. If things got heavy, she wasn't afraid to fight, whether she needed to pull a knife or a pistol."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Impatience in the Studio
xref.body: Known for his lack of patience during recording sessions, particularly if a take was prolonged. His impatience led him to instruct a tape op to erase the "Where the Streets Have No Name" track for U2 when the band struggled with its time signature changes. "Eno doesn’t have a lot of patience. So if something takes too long, he probably thinks there’s something wrong with that and we should just move on to something else"

xref.title: Jerry Dammers' Background and Motivation
xref.body: Founder Jerry Dammers, born in India and the ex-hippie son of a missionary minister, was deeply influenced by the diverse music heard on the streets of Coventry. He used music to rebel against his father and to push back against the bleak working-class existence of his city, embracing punk's freedom of expression. "Jerry Damers was born in India and the ex-Hippie son of a missionary minister. He was a huge fan of all this music that he was hearing in the street. He was also very much into the freedom of expression that came with the punk movement of the 1970s."

xref.title: Musical Development in England
xref.body: While in England, Dillon honed his songwriting skills and gained confidence performing covers and his own music on the streets, a period crucial to his development as a frontman and lyricist. "I'd learned to write songs and play on the street in England. And I was playing covers and stuff. So I had no compunction in terms of playing my own music."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: New York City Origins and Controversial Subject Matter
xref.body: Emerging from the streets of New York City in 1966, The Velvet Underground, featuring Lou Reed, was deemed too unconventional for mainstream appeal. Their music, characterized by its "weirdness," openly addressed taboo subjects like sex and drugs, which were largely unaccepted in rock and roll at the time. This thematic content, more so than Lou Reed's vocal style, was a primary reason for their non-mainstream status. "Lou and the Velvet were from the streets of New York City and were just too weird for mainstream consumption."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: New York Underground Origins
xref.body: Unlike Bob Dylan, who came from the folk scene and secured a major record deal, Lou Reed and The Velvet Underground originated from the streets of New York City and were deemed too unconventional for mainstream consumption, especially due to their explicit subject matter. "Lou and the Velvet were from the streets of New York City and were just too weird for mainstream consumption."

xref.title: Performance Spill-Over and Police Intervention
xref.body: His chaotic performances often extended into the streets, and police presence was a regular occurrence at his shows due to their extreme nature. "Sometimes his performances would spill out onto the street. And always, always, always. He was threatening suicide. Sometimes he promised that he would take people with him. So no wonder cops were a regular thing at his shows."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Pioneers of Rap/Hip Hop
xref.body: Grandmaster Flash was a key figure who emerged from the nascent rap and hip hop scene on the streets of New York, where DJs developed techniques of "turntableism" by chopping and manipulating records to create new sounds for MCs to rhyme over. "This is the culture that gave us run DMC and Grandmaster Flash."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Punk Roots and NYC Influence
xref.body: The Beastie Boys initially began as a punk band but evolved their sound after becoming fascinated with the music emerging from the projects and streets of New York clubs. "The Beastie Boys originally started as a punk band, but as they spent more time in the clubs of New York, they became fascinated with the music that was coming from the projects in the streets."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Shane MacGowan's Funeral
xref.body: Following Shane MacGowan's death in Dublin on November 30, 2023, he received a massive public sendoff, with people lining the streets to pay their respects to his funeral procession. "When Shane died in Dublin on November 30, 2023, he was given a massive sendoff as people line the streets to give the respects to the funeral procession."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: World's First Recording Star
xref.body: George W. Johnson, a former slave freed around 1853, became the world's first recording star and biggest pop star in the late 1890s. He sang on the streets of New York City before being recruited in 1890 by Charles Marshall to make recordings for coin-operated phonographs. "George W. Johnson was the world's first and biggest pop star in the late 1890s."
